Evaluate the left-hand side of the $z$-equation using $s = -1$:
$$\text{LHS} = 2 + 3(-1) = 2 - 3 = -1$$

Evaluate the right-hand side of the $z$-equation using $t = -3$:
$$\text{RHS} = 4 + 4(-3) = 4 - 12 = -8$$

State the conclusion:
Since $\text{LHS} \neq \text{RHS}$ ($-1 \neq -8$), the system of equations is inconsistent, proving that the two lines do not intersect.

walkthrough.text:
Set up and solve the $x$ and $y$ component equations:
$$x: 1 + \lambda = 4 - \mu \implies \lambda + \mu = 3 \quad \text{--- (1)}$$
$$y: 1 + 2\lambda = 2 + 3\mu \implies 2\lambda - 3\mu = 1 \quad \text{--- (2)}$$

Multiply (1) by 3 and add to (2):
$$3(\lambda + \mu) + (2\lambda - 3\mu) = 9 + 1 \implies 5\lambda = 10 \implies \lambda = 2$$
$$\mu = 3 - 2 = 1$$

Substitute $\lambda = 2$ and $\mu = 1$ into the $z$-equation to find $p$:
$$1 + p(2) = 2 + 5(1) \implies 1 + 2p = 7 \implies 2p = 6 \implies p = 3$$

walkthrough.text:
Set up and solve simultaneous equations from the $x$ and $y$ components:
$$x: 1 + 2s = 2 + t \implies t = 2s - 1 \quad \text{--- (1)}$$
$$y: 3 - s = 1 - t \quad \text{--- (2)}$$
$$3 - s = 1 - (2s - 1) = 2 - 2s \implies s = -1$$
$$t = 2(-1) - 1 = -3$$

Test in the third ($z$) component equation:
$$\text{LHS} = 2 + 3(-1) = -1$$
$$\text{RHS} = 4 + 4(-3) = -8$$
Since $\text{LHS} \neq \text{RHS}$ ($-1 \neq -8$), there is no simultaneous solution.

Conclude the geometric classification:
Because the lines are neither parallel nor intersecting, $l_1$ and $l_2$ are skew lines.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Skew lines proof with fractional parameters.

walkthrough.text:
Check whether direction vectors are parallel:
$$\mathbf{d}_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{d}_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix} \implies \frac{2}{1} \neq \frac{-1}{2}$$
The direction vectors are not parallel.

Set up and solve the $x$ and $y$ component equations:
$$x: 1 + 2\lambda = 2 + \mu \implies \mu = 2\lambda - 1 \quad \text{--- (1)}$$
$$y: 2 - \lambda = 1 + 2\mu \quad \text{--- (2)}$$
$$2 - \lambda = 1 + 2(2\lambda - 1) = 4\lambda - 1 \implies 5\lambda = 3 \implies \lambda = \frac{3}{5}$$
$$\mu = 2\left(\frac{3}{5}\right) - 1 = \frac{1}{5}$$

Substitute into the $z$-component equation:
$$\text{LHS} = -1 + 2\left(\frac{3}{5}\right) = \frac{1}{5}$$
$$\text{RHS} = 4 - 1\left(\frac{1}{5}\right) = \frac{19}{5}$$
Since $\text{LHS} \neq \text{RHS}$ ($\frac{1}{5} \neq \frac{19}{5}$), the lines do not intersect.

Conclude:
Since the lines are non-parallel and non-intersecting, $AB$ and $l$ are skew lines.

parts.label: (b)
hints: Since $-\frac{2}{7} \neq \frac{19}{7}$, conclude that the lines do not intersect.

walkthrough.text:
Set up parametric equations for $x$ and $y$:
$$x: 1 + \lambda = 3 + 2\mu \implies \lambda - 2\mu = 2 \quad \text{--- (1)}$$
$$y: 2 - 3\lambda = 1 + \mu \implies 3\lambda + \mu = 1 \quad \text{--- (2)}$$

Multiply (1) by 3 and subtract from (2):
$$3(\lambda - 2\mu) = 3\lambda - 6\mu = 6$$
$$(3\lambda + \mu) - (3\lambda - 6\mu) = 1 - 6 \implies 7\mu = -5 \implies \mu = -\frac{5}{7}$$
$$\lambda = 2 + 2\left(-\frac{5}{7}\right) = \frac{4}{7}$$

Test $\lambda = \frac{4}{7}$ and $\mu = -\frac{5}{7}$ in the $z$-equation:
$$\text{LHS} = -2 + 3\left(\frac{4}{7}\right) = -\frac{14}{7} + \frac{12}{7} = -\frac{2}{7}$$
$$\text{RHS} = 2 - 1\left(-\frac{5}{7}\right) = \frac{14}{7} + \frac{5}{7} = \frac{19}{7}$$

State the conclusion:
Since $\text{LHS} \neq \text{RHS}$ ($-\frac{2}{7} \neq \frac{19}{7}$), the three component equations are inconsistent, proving that the lines do not intersect.

questions.difficulty_reason: Core: Comprehensive skew lines proof with clean integer steps.

walkthrough.text:
Compare the direction vectors of $l_1$ and $l_2$:
$$\mathbf{d}_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \\ 3 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{d}_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix} \implies \frac{1}{2} \neq \frac{2}{1}$$
Since $\mathbf{d}_1 \neq k\mathbf{d}_2$, the lines are not parallel.

State the three component equations for intersection:
$$x: 4 + s = 1 + 2t \quad \text{--- (1)}$$
$$y: 2 + 2s = -1 + t \quad \text{--- (2)}$$
$$z: 1 + 3s = 2 - t \quad \text{--- (3)}$$

Solve equations (1) and (2) simultaneously:
$$s - 2t = -3 \implies s = 2t - 3$$
$$2(2t - 3) - t = -3 \implies 4t - 6 - t = -3 \implies 3t = 3 \implies t = 1$$
$$s = 2(1) - 3 = -1$$

Test $s = -1$ and $t = 1$ in equation (3):
$$\text{LHS} = 1 + 3(-1) = -2$$
$$\text{RHS} = 2 - (1) = 1$$
Since $\text{LHS} \neq \text{RHS}$ ($-2 \neq 1$), the equations are inconsistent.

Conclude the proof:
Because the lines are neither parallel nor intersecting, $l_1$ and $l_2$ are skew lines.

questions.difficulty_reason: Capstone: 4-way line relationship classification suite (coincident vs intersecting).

walkthrough.text:
Compare the direction vectors of $l_1$ and $l_2$:
$$\mathbf{d}_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 2 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix} = 2\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix} = 2\mathbf{d}_1$$
Since $\mathbf{d}_2 = 2\mathbf{d}_1$, the lines have identical direction.

Test whether the base point $(3, 1, 1)$ of line $l_2$ lies on line $l_1$:
$$x: 1 + 2\lambda = 3 \implies \lambda = 1$$
$$y: 0 + 1(1) = 1$$
$$z: 2 - 1(1) = 1$$
Since $\lambda = 1$ consistently yields $(3, 1, 1)$, every point on $l_2$ lies on $l_1$.

Conclude:
Lines $l_1$ and $l_2$ are coincident lines (they represent the exact same line in space).

Since $z$-equation is consistent, $l_1$ and $l_3$ are intersecting at $\left(\frac{5}{3}, \frac{1}{3}, \frac{5}{3}\right)$.

walkthrough.text:
Compare direction vectors:
$$\mathbf{d}_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{d}_3 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \\ -2 \end{pmatrix} \implies \frac{2}{1} \neq \frac{1}{-1}$$
The lines $l_1$ and $l_3$ are not parallel.

Set up and solve $x$ and $y$ equations:
$$x: 1 + 2\lambda = \nu \quad \text{--- (1)}$$
$$y: \lambda = 2 - \nu \quad \text{--- (2)}$$
$$\lambda = 2 - (1 + 2\lambda) = 1 - 2\lambda \implies 3\lambda = 1 \implies \lambda = \frac{1}{3}$$
$$\nu = 1 + 2\left(\frac{1}{3}\right) = \frac{5}{3}$$

Verify in the $z$-component equation:
$$\text{LHS} = 2 - \lambda = 2 - \frac{1}{3} = \frac{5}{3}$$
$$\text{RHS} = 5 - 2\nu = 5 - 2\left(\frac{5}{3}\right) = \frac{5}{3}$$
Since $\text{LHS} = \text{RHS} = \frac{5}{3}$, the lines intersect.

State the conclusion:
Lines $l_1$ and $l_3$ are **intersecting lines**, meeting at the point $\left(\frac{5}{3}, \frac{1}{3}, \frac{5}{3}\right)$.

parts.label: (a)
hints: Direction vectors are $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$, which are non-parallel ($\mathbf{i} \neq k\mathbf{j}$).

walkthrough.text:
Compare the direction vectors of $l_1$ and $l_2$:
$$\mathbf{d}_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} = \mathbf{i}, \quad \mathbf{d}_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} = \mathbf{j}$$
Since unit vectors along orthogonal axes are not scalar multiples, the lines are not parallel.

Set up component equations for intersection:
$$x: \lambda = 0 \implies \lambda = 0$$
$$y: 0 = \mu \implies \mu = 0$$
$$z: 10 = 0$$

Show the contradiction and conclude:
The $z$-equation yields $10 = 0$, which is impossible ($10 \neq 0$).
Because the lines are neither parallel nor intersecting, they are skew lines.

parts.label: (b)
hints: Since $\lambda^2 \ge 0$ and $\mu^2 \ge 0$, minimum occurs at $\lambda = \mu = 0$, giving distance $\sqrt{100} = 10$.

walkthrough.text:
Express the displacement vector $\vec{PQ}$ between a general point $P(\lambda, 0, 10)$ on $l_1$ and $Q(0, \mu, 0)$ on $l_2$:
$$\vec{PQ} = \mathbf{q} - \mathbf{p} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 - \lambda \\ \mu - 0 \\ 0 - 10 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} -\lambda \\ \mu \\ -10 \end{pmatrix}$$

Compute the squared distance between $P$ and $Q$:
$$|\vec{PQ}|^2 = (-\lambda)^2 + \mu^2 + (-10)^2 = \lambda^2 + \mu^2 + 100$$

Find the minimum distance:
Since $\lambda^2 \ge 0$ and $\mu^2 \ge 0$ for all real numbers, the sum $\lambda^2 + \mu^2 + 100$ achieves its absolute minimum when $\lambda = 0$ and $\mu = 0$:
$$|\vec{PQ}|_{\text{min}} = \sqrt{0 + 0 + 100} = 10$$

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Acute angle between direction vectors of skew lines.

walkthrough.text:
Compute the scalar product and magnitudes of the direction vectors:
$$\mathbf{d}_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{d}_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ -3 \end{pmatrix}$$
$$\mathbf{d}_1 \cdot \mathbf{d}_2 = 1(1) + 0(1) + 0(-3) = 1$$
$$|\mathbf{d}_1| = 1, \quad |\mathbf{d}_2| = \sqrt{1^2 + 1^2 + (-3)^2} = \sqrt{1 + 1 + 9} = \sqrt{11}$$

Evaluate the acute angle $\theta$:
$$\cos\theta = \frac{|\mathbf{d}_1 \cdot \mathbf{d}_2|}{|\mathbf{d}_1| |\mathbf{d}_2|} = \frac{1}{1 \times \sqrt{11}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{11}}$$
$$\theta = \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{11}}\right) \approx 72.5^\circ$$
